source: Schaeffer et al. (2025) How Do Large Language Monkeys Get Their Power (Laws)?
finding: On each single problem the failure rate falls exponentially with the number of independent attempts. The aggregate power law over many problems comes from a heavy left tail in the distribution of single-attempt success probabilities (a few problems with very low pass@1).
numbers: Tested on Pythia 70M to 12B (math) and best-of-N jailbreaking of GPT4o, Claude 3.5, Gemini 1.5, Llama 3 8B IT. Pass@1 distributions fit by scaled Beta distributions. Llama 3 8B IT has no power-law tail and shows no aggregate power law. Forecasting the exponent needs 2 to 4 orders of magnitude less compute than least squares (paper claim).
quote: per-problem exponential scaling can be made consistent with aggregate polynomial scaling if the distribution of single-attempt success probabilities is heavy tailed
limits: The heavy tail is over items (pass@1 across problems), not over run time within one attempt. Attempt count is the unit, not tokens. Does not measure finishing time or hazard of one attempt.
agent_relevance: For one fixed item, fresh attempts behave like a constant per-attempt success chance, so restart gains within an item come from the item-level mixture, not from a falling hazard across attempts. This partly answers gap 1 at the attempt level. The within-attempt token hazard is still unmeasured.

source: Olausson et al. (2024) Is Self-Repair a Silver Bullet for Code Generation? (ICLR 2024)
finding: At equal sample budget, repair with unit-test results plus a model-written explanation often does not beat plain i.i.d. resampling, especially at small budgets. Spending budget on diverse first drafts beats spending it on many repairs of few drafts.
numbers: CodeLlama-13b-instruct, GPT-3.5, GPT-4 on HumanEval and 300 APPS tasks; Np=50 draws. GPT-4 on APPS: 10 drafts + 1 repair each (up to 20 samples) is 1.05x the pass@20 baseline; 2 drafts + 10 repairs each (22 samples) is 0.97x of pass@22. On APPS only GPT-4 gains clearly; Code Llama and GPT-3.5 mostly match or lag the baseline. Gains at small budgets are marginal or absent. An appendix pass@t metric counts tokens and shows the same trends.
quote: self-repair is not a silver bullet
limits: 2023-era models, single-turn repair, feedback is the same model's explanation of the test failure. Not reasoning models. Main budget counted in samples, not tokens.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence for gap 7: tool output alone (test failure plus self-explanation) is not enough to beat fresh restarts at equal budget. Default for the schema: several short fresh attempts first, repair only the most promising draft.

source: Olausson et al. (2024) feedback-quality experiments
finding: The bottleneck of repair is the quality of the feedback. A stronger model or a human writing the explanation lifts repair clearly above both the baseline and self-repair.
numbers: Repair success of failing GPT-4 programs: 33.3% with GPT-4 feedback vs 52.6% with human feedback (1.58x). By difficulty: introductory 42.64 vs 62.21; interview 19.33 vs 45.67; competition 3.67 vs 14.67. Code Llama with GPT-3.5 or GPT-4 feedback, and GPT-3.5 with GPT-4 feedback, beat both baseline and self-repair at all budgets.
limits: Human feedback is costly and not a scaffold option. The stronger-model result needs a second, stronger model.
agent_relevance: A better critic (a bigger model, or code that names the fault) is what makes continue-with-feedback beat restart. Raw error text alone is not shown to be enough.

source: Huang (2007) The Effect of Restarts on the Efficiency of Clause Learning (IJCAI-07)
finding: In a clause-learning SAT solver (TINISAT), every restart policy beats no restarts by a wide margin. Luby is best of six restart policies on the whole suite, but only by a small margin over the best fixed cutoff.
numbers: 22 industrial families, 251 instances, 2 h cutoff. Solved (of 251): N none 127, M geometric (100,1.5) 164, Z (700,1) 166, B (550,1) 168, G (32,1.1) 174, S fixed 16000 178, L Luby unit 32 180; MiniSat 128; Siege 182. Total time in days: N 11.28, M 8.85, Z 8.49, B 8.56, G 8.00, S 7.80, L 7.68; MiniSat 11.45; Siege 7.45. Worst restart policy finished 2.43 days sooner and solved 37 more than no restarts. No policy is best on every family.
limits: One solver, one benchmark suite. Learned clauses persist across restarts, so this is not amnesiac restarting. Luby beats fixed-16000 by 2 instances and 0.12 days, a small edge.
agent_relevance: Closes the Huang part of gap 10 (tables read from the primary PDF). Luby is a safe default, not a large win over a well-chosen fixed unit.

source: Huang (2007) tables 2 and 3 and Luby definition
finding: Per-family gaps between policies are larger than the aggregate. The paper states the Luby sequence and the 1993 optimality result: expected time within a log factor of the best distribution-specific policy, and no universal policy better by more than a constant.
numbers: Luby: t_i = 2^(k-1) if i = 2^k - 1, else t_(i-2^(k-1)+1) if 2^(k-1) <= i < 2^k - 1 (sequence 1,1,2,1,1,2,4,...). fvp-unsat-2.0 total time: N 1383.53 s, M 1193.24 s, L (Luby) 469.3 s; L beats M by 2.5x there but only 1.2x overall. vliw-sat-4.0 (satisfiable): N 10546.68 s vs one restart policy 2028.97 s.
quote: no other universal policy can do better by more than a constant factor
limits: A restatement of Luby et al. 1993, not the proof. The paper says the relevance of the theorem to clause learning is an open question. The 1993 paper itself could not be opened.
agent_relevance: Constants for the schema text are confirmed from a primary secondary-source: 1,1,2,1,1,2,4 times a unit. The log-factor guarantee holds for independent Las Vegas runs only.

source: Lecoutre, Sais, Tabary, Vidal (2007) Nogood Recording from Restarts (IJCAI-07)
finding: Plain restarts in a CSP solver can hurt. Recording a small set of nogoods (failed decision sequences from the last branch) at each restart removes repeated work and gives a modest gain.
numbers: 1064 instances of the 2005 CSP competition, 30 min limit. Timeouts / avg time in s for MAC, MAC+restart, MAC+restart+nogoods: dom/ddeg 365/125.0, 378/159.0, 337/109.1; brelaz 277/85.1, 298/121.7, 261/78.2; dom/wdeg 140/47.8, 123/56.0, 121/43.6. (Column grouping reconstructed from the text; restart alone raised time under all three heuristics and raised timeouts under the two classical ones.)
limits: Column reading from PDF text is partly reconstructed. CSP, not LLM. Nogoods are verified-false facts, a different object from a prior answer.
agent_relevance: Supports gap 4: what crosses a restart should be verified negative knowledge (what failed), which cannot anchor the next attempt toward a wrong answer.

source: Lecoutre et al. (2007) hard instances and the small-kernel failure
finding: Restarts lose on instances with a small hidden unsatisfiable core when the heuristic does not point at it (series ehi): restarting is pure expense. On hard real-world RLFAP instances restarts give about one order of magnitude, nogoods a further 10 percent.
numbers: MAC+restart with brelaz (dom/ddeg) solved 27 (32) fewer instances than MAC on the ehi series. RLFAP scen11-f1 (680 variables, domain up to 43) solved in 36 runs with only 712 nogoods, average size 8.5, max 33.
limits: One benchmark family explains the loss. The dom/wdeg heuristic made restarts robust even on ehi.
agent_relevance: A boundary condition: if early search has no information about where the hard core is, restart is a pure cost. Learned failure weights (dom/wdeg) fix this. In agent terms, carry failure counts or error tags across attempts.

source: Madaan et al. (2025) Rethinking Thinking Tokens: LLMs as Improvement Operators (Parallel-Distill-Refine)
finding: At matched sequential budget, iterative pipelines beat one long chain of thought; parallel drafts plus a distilled summary (PDR) give the largest gain. When ALL tokens are counted, sequential refinement (SR) is on the Pareto frontier and parallel drafts do not pay.
numbers: AIME 2024 and 2025, o3-mini and gemini-2.5-flash, mean over 16 runs. o3-mini at effective budget 49k tokens (16k per call): Long CoT 76.9, SR 81.5, PDR 86.7. Headline: PDR +11 points on AIME 2024 and +9 on AIME 2025 for their RL-trained 8B model at matched sequential budget. Figure 4 caption: for Btotal, SR forms the Pareto frontier because there are no parallel drafts.
quote: for Btotal, SR forms the pareto-frontier
limits: Symbolic verifiers (math). Sequential-budget accounting favours parallel; total-token accounting does not. Reasoning models only.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: under equal TOTAL tokens, refining one candidate with a re-check beats a long single chain and is not beaten by k parallel drafts; parallel drafts help latency. In our token-limited agent, restart should be justified by stuck evidence, not by default.

source: Madaan et al. (2025) PDR oracle workspace experiment (anchoring)
finding: What is carried into the next round matters a lot. Summaries built only from wrong drafts sharply cut accuracy; summaries built only from correct drafts raise it above random selection. The drop is larger for the model with weaker self-verification.
numbers: Three-round PDR, [16, 8, 4] generations per round, top-k with k=2; policies Random-k, Oracle-Incorrect, Oracle-Correct; gemini-2.5-flash and o3-mini; AIME 2024 and 2025. Reported as large drops for Oracle-Incorrect, larger for o3-mini (values only in figures, not recorded).
limits: Oracle selection is not available at run time. Exact numbers not read from the figure.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: anchoring is real and measurable. Carry only what code has verified (or nothing). A prior answer without a check is a bet on the model's own judge.

source: Think Twice: Enhancing LLM Reasoning by Scaling Multi-round Test-time Thinking (2025)
finding: Giving a reasoning model its previous answer and asking it to re-answer, with no verifier, gives small gains over round 1 on hard math and code, flattening after a few rounds.
numbers: AIME 2024 pass@1 (32 samples per query): QwQ-32B 80.3 to 82.1 (round 2) to 83.1 (round 4); DeepSeek-R1 79.7 to 82.0; another model 72.8 to 76.7. GPQA-Diamond R1 74.0 to 74.8; LiveCodeBench R1 65.3 to 67.1; MATH-500 R1 flat at 97.6.
quote: The assistant's previous answer is: <answer> last round answer </answer>, and please re-answer.
limits: Round 2 costs about twice the tokens of round 1 and there is NO equal-token control (for example best of two fresh samples). Gains are 1 to 4 points on 30 AIME items. No verifier.
agent_relevance: Carrying the prior answer does not collapse into pure anchoring for strong reasoning models, but gives no evidence it beats a fresh restart. Gap 4 stays open on the equal-token comparison.

source: Ghosal et al. (2025) Does Thinking More Always Help? Mirage of Test-Time Scaling in Reasoning Models
finding: Extending thinking with Wait first raises then lowers accuracy. At a fixed token budget, several independent paths with a self-agreement vote beat Wait-extension. The authors explain the hump by rising output variance.
numbers: DeepSeek-R1-Distill 1.5B, 7B, Llama-8B on GSM8K, MATH-500, AIME 2024. One model on GSM8K: accuracy 82.2 to 87.3 as average thinking tokens rose, then fell to 70.3 as tokens went from 1,100 to 15,980. At a 16K budget parallel thinking is about 22 percent higher than Wait & Think More and 47 percent higher than exact-thinking budget control.
limits: Small distilled models; the vote uses model-likelihood self-agreement. Wait-forcing is a cruder form of continue than natural continuation.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: supports splitting a long budget into several short attempts for small reasoning models. Combined with d08, the answer depends on whether the continuation includes a real check.

source: Zeng et al. (2025) Revisiting the Test-Time Scaling of o1-like Models
finding: For the same question, correct solutions are often shorter than incorrect ones. Longer chains contain more self-revisions, and these rarely turn wrong answers right (some models turn right answers wrong more often). Parallel sampling gives better coverage than sequential revision.
numbers: QwQ, R1 family, LIMO. R1-Distill-14b/32b and LIMO improved in early revisions then oscillated; QwQ and R1-Distill-1.5b degraded as reflection length grew. Coverage compared with 10 parallel solutions against 10 sequential revisions (values in figures only).
limits: Exact accuracy numbers are in figures, not read. Self-revision without an external check.
agent_relevance: Gaps 6 and 7: without an external signal, continuing is a worse use of tokens than restart for most models tested. A chain longer than the typical correct one is a cheap stop signal computable in code.

source: Muennighoff et al. (2025) s1: Simple test-time scaling
finding: Forcing the model to continue with Wait raises AIME slightly and flattens. Sampling until a generation is short (rejection by length) shows inverse scaling: shorter allowed thinking gave higher accuracy.
numbers: s1-32B appendix table AIME24 / AIME25: no budget forcing 50.0 / 26.7; Wait 1x 53.3 / 30.0; 2x 53.3 / 33.3; 4x 56.7 / 36.7. MATH500 92.6, 92.8, 93.0, 92.2; GPQA 56.6, 59.6, 59.6, 58.6. Rejection sampling needed average 655, 97, 8, 3, 2 and 1 tries per sample for the limits listed (3500 to 16000 thinking tokens; list as printed); accuracy fell as allowed length rose. 12 of 30 questions overflowed context when prompted for 512 steps.
limits: 30 questions per AIME set, so one item is 3.3 points. Single model. REBASE with a process reward model scaled better than both.
agent_relevance: The Wait gain is within 1 to 3 items; a continue rule should not rest on it. Rejection-by-length suggests an attempt that has run long has a lower chance of ending right: a falling hazard of success per added token (indirect evidence for gap 1).

source: Fu et al. (2025) Deep Think with Confidence (DeepConf)
finding: A within-trace stop signal built from token confidence in a sliding window (lowest group confidence, window 2,048 tokens), with a threshold set from 16 warm-up traces, cuts tokens of parallel reasoning by 43 to 79 percent (DeepConf-low) or 18 to 59 percent (DeepConf-high) at about the same accuracy.
numbers: Budget K=512 traces; DeepSeek-8B, Qwen3-8B/32B, GPT-OSS-20B/120B on AIME24, AIME25, BRUMO25, HMMT25. Up to 84.7 percent fewer tokens (GPT-OSS-120B AIME 2025; offline accuracy 99.9 vs 97.0 for majority voting). DeepSeek-8B AIME24 +5.8 points; Qwen3-32B BRUMO25 -0.9. Mean token savings on DeepSeek-8B 62.88 percent (low), 47.67 percent (high). Consensus stop threshold 0.95 on Qwen3-32B AIME24: 52.8 percent fewer tokens at B=512, accuracy unchanged; 0.90 gave -0.26 points.
quote: DeepConf-low reduces tokens by 43-79% across AIME24/AIME25/BRUMO25/HMMT25
limits: Needs token log-probabilities and 16 warm-up traces per prompt. Overconfident wrong traces (GPT-OSS-120B) defeat it. The signal is read after thousands of tokens, not the first few hundred. Compared against majority voting, not against Luby.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: an LLM analogue of Kautz's early-signal predictor exists and works on math reasoning models. Not tested at the first few hundred tokens, nor against Luby at equal tokens. Needs logprobs, which a hosted agent may not expose.

source: Aggarwal, Madaan, Yang, Mausam (2023) Let's Sample Step by Step: Adaptive-Consistency
finding: Stop sampling when the lead of the top answer is statistically safe (a Dirichlet model of answer counts). A code-only stop signal based on answer agreement across attempts.
numbers: 17 reasoning and code datasets, three LLMs: sample budget cut by up to 7.9x with average accuracy drop under 0.1 percent. Works best where a clear majority appears within 5 samples.
limits: Needs a closed answer space so answers can be compared. 2022 to 2023 models, no reasoning models. Saves cost; does not show that restart beats continue.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: answer unchanged across restarts is a validated stop signal for the number of attempts (not for aborting one attempt). Fits ARC-style outputs, where grids compare by code.

source: Li et al. (2024) Escape Sky-high Cost: Early-stopping Self-Consistency (ESC), ICLR 2024
finding: Sample in small windows and stop as soon as one window is unanimous. Cuts samples at comparable accuracy on six benchmarks.
numbers: Average sample reduction: MATH -33.8 percent, GSM8K -80.1, StrategyQA -76.8, CommonsenseQA -78.5, Coin Flip -84.2, Last Letters -67.4. Window size 5 (8 for MATH), averaged over 10 runs.
limits: Different group from d15, same idea, so they corroborate each other. Fixed-vote tasks; no verifier.
agent_relevance: Second independent source for agreement-based stopping. The saving is large on easy items and about one third on hard MATH.

source: Han et al. (2024) Token-Budget-Aware LLM Reasoning (TALE)
finding: Telling the model a token budget in the prompt compresses chain of thought, but a budget that is too small makes the model use more tokens than a larger budget does (token elasticity). The budget the model sees changes its behaviour in a non-monotonic way.
numbers: TALE-EP: on average 67 percent fewer output tokens with under 3 percent accuracy loss; TALE-PT: about 50 percent fewer tokens than vanilla CoT. Optimal budget found by binary search per question.
limits: Non-reasoning chat models, one-shot budget statements, not attempt counters. No restart.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: a visible budget can backfire when it is below what the task needs. Show attempts left and tokens left, but do not set the visible per-attempt budget below the typical solved length. Does not test giving up early.

source: Setlur et al. (2025) Scaling Test-Time Compute Without Verification or RL is Suboptimal
finding: Theory and experiments say that test-time search guided by a verifier beats imitating good traces without a verifier, and the gap widens as test compute grows when the base model has a spread of correct solution styles.
numbers: 3B, 8B, 32B models on math; compares s1-style distillation with best-of-N search. The paper proves the gap and reports it growing with budget (figure values not read).
limits: Concerns fine-tuning as well as inference. Does not study restart schedules.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: without a verifier signal no restart schedule is expected to dominate. Convert as much as possible into code-checkable signals (run the candidate, check on the examples) before relying on restart rules.

source: Zilberstein (1996) Using Anytime Algorithms in Intelligent Systems (AI Magazine 17(3))
finding: Only the publisher landing page and abstract were read. The PDF download returned an empty body from the publisher site (several tries, with cookies). The abstract says anytime algorithms trade deliberation time for quality of results and the article surveys the metalevel control problem of composing several anytime algorithms.
numbers: none
limits: The property list (measurable quality, recognisable quality, monotonicity, consistency, diminishing returns, interruptibility, preemptability) was NOT verified from the text.
agent_relevance: Gap 10 stays open for the property list. Mark the schema text as standard anytime properties from memory until a copy is opened.

source: Wikipedia (accessed 2026-10-26) Anytime algorithm
finding: The article names measurable quality (citing Zilberstein 1996) and interruptibility (citing Grass 1996), contrasts anytime with contract algorithms that must declare a time in advance, and does not name monotonicity, diminishing returns or preemptability as listed properties. Dean and Boddy 1988 is not cited; only Boddy and Dean 1989 is under further reading.
numbers: none
limits: Secondary source, used only to show the property list cannot be fixed from the open web summary.
agent_relevance: Do not cite a numbered property list in the schema as from Zilberstein 1996 until the primary text is read. Keep the two properties actually needed: returns best-so-far when interrupted, and quality is measurable by code.
